{{Short description|Conjecture in number theory mathematics}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Feit–Thompson conjecture''' is a  [[conjecture]] in [[number theory]], suggested by  {{harvs|txt=yes|first=Walter|last= Feit|authorlink=Walter Feit| first2=John G. |last2=Thompson|author2-link=John G. Thompson|year=1962}}. The conjecture states that there are no distinct [[prime number]]s ''p'' and ''q'' such that
:<math>\frac{p^{q} - 1}{p - 1}</math> divides <math>\frac{q^{p} - 1}{q - 1}</math>.

If the conjecture were true, it would greatly simplify the final chapter of the [[mathematical proof|proof]] {{harv|Feit|Thompson|1963}} of the [[Feit–Thompson theorem]] that every [[finite group]] of odd [[order (group theory)|order]] is [[solvable group|solvable]].  A stronger conjecture that the two numbers are always [[coprime integers|coprime]] was disproved  by {{harvtxt|Stephens|1971}} with the [[counterexample]] ''p''&nbsp;=&nbsp;17 and ''q''&nbsp;=&nbsp;3313 with common [[divisor|factor]] 2''pq''&nbsp;+&thinsp;1&nbsp;=&nbsp;112643.

It is known that the conjecture is true for ''q''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2&nbsp;{{harv|Stephens|1971}} and ''q''&nbsp;=&nbsp;3&nbsp;{{harv|Le|2012}}.

Informal [[probability]] arguments suggest that the "expected" number of counterexamples to the Feit–Thompson conjecture is very close to 0, suggesting that the Feit–Thompson conjecture is likely to be true.
